what: Sabra Health Care REIT owns healthcare property. It buys skilled nursing homes, assisted living and memory care facilities, behavioural health hospitals and medical offices, and leases them to operators who run the care. It owns the buildings; it does not provide the care itself.
customers: Healthcare operators who run nursing homes, senior housing and behavioural health facilities and pay rent under long leases, plus some properties where Sabra takes a share of the operating result.
money: Rent from skilled nursing, behavioural health and senior housing operators under long leases.
Properties where Sabra takes the operating economics rather than a fixed rent.
Interest on loans to operators and other investments.
moat: Healthcare property is specialised: a skilled nursing facility cannot easily become anything else, and the licences attached to it are themselves valuable and limited by state. Leases are long and triple-net, meaning the operator pays taxes, insurance and maintenance, so the landlord’s cash flow is unusually clean once the rent is being paid.
risks: The tenants are the whole risk: nursing home operators run on thin margins funded largely by Medicaid, and when an operator fails the landlord must find another or take the property back.
Reported net income of $71.5M gives a price/earnings ratio of 73.1, though property depreciation makes earnings a poor measure for a property company.
Free cash flow was about negative $267.1M, reflecting property acquisitions rather than operating weakness.
Debt of $2.5B against $71.5M of cash is substantial and must be refinanced periodically.
Medicaid reimbursement rates are set by state governments under budget pressure, and they determine whether operators can pay rent.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year, from $569.5M in 2021 to $774.6M in 2025, with trailing revenue of $919.1M.
America’s population over eighty is growing rapidly, which is the demand driver for every property type Sabra owns.
Triple-net leases mean the operator pays taxes, insurance and maintenance, leaving the landlord a clean rent stream.
Very little new skilled nursing capacity is being built, so existing facilities face limited new competition.
Fourteen analysts average a $22.93 target, about 12% above the current price.
watch: Rent coverage ratios at the operator level. A landlord is only as safe as its tenants’ ability to pay, and coverage tells you how much cushion there is before rent stops.
view: Owning healthcare property looks like a demographic certainty and is in fact a credit analysis. The demographics are genuine — the population over eighty in America is growing quickly, very little new skilled nursing capacity is being built, and demand for these facilities will exceed supply for decades. None of that helps if the operator running the building cannot pay the rent.

And the operators are financially fragile by construction. Skilled nursing is funded largely by Medicaid, at rates set by state governments under permanent budget pressure, against labour costs that have risen sharply and a chronic shortage of nurses. Operators run on thin margins in good conditions. When one fails, the landlord does not simply find a replacement: the building is specialised, the licence is state-controlled, and the transition takes time during which rent stops. This is why rent coverage ratios — how much the operator earns relative to the rent owed — are the only metric that genuinely matters here.

The lease structure is favourable where it works. Triple-net means the operator pays taxes, insurance and maintenance, so the rent arrives clean with no landlord obligations attached. The senior housing operating portfolio is a different proposition: there Sabra takes the operating economics directly, which means more upside when occupancy is strong and direct exposure to labour costs when it is not.

On the figures, ignore the 73 times price/earnings ratio — property depreciation that bears no relation to economic wear makes earnings meaningless for a REIT, and the negative free cash flow is acquisitions rather than trouble. What is real is $2.5 billion of debt against $71.5 million of cash, which means refinancing is a recurring event decided by the bond market. Revenue growth from $570 million to $919 million shows the acquisition programme working. I would hold this for the demographics and watch coverage ratios obsessively, because that is where the warning comes from.
bull: An ageing population meets almost no new supply, operators’ rent coverage holds, and acquisitions keep compounding a portfolio of specialised, irreplaceable buildings.
bear: Medicaid rates lag labour costs, an operator fails and rent stops on specialised buildings that are hard to re-tenant, with $2.5 billion of debt still due.
